questions.question: Identify the sentence without the adverbial error.
questions.questionHtml: Identify the sentence without the adverbial error.

options.text: She ran the marathon fast incredibly.
options.html: She ran the marathon fast incredibly.

options.text: She ran the marathon incredibly fast.
options.html: She ran the marathon incredibly fast.

options.text: She ran incredibly the marathon fast.
options.html: She ran incredibly the marathon fast.

options.text: She ran the incredibly marathon fast.
options.html: She ran the incredibly marathon fast.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is '2' i.e. She ran the marathon incredibly fast.

Key Points

  • The adverbial error in the sentence is due to the incorrect placement of the adverbs "fast" and "incredibly".
  • In English, adverbs of manner (like "fast") typically come after the main verb or the object if there is one.
  • When using two adverbs to describe how something is done, the adverb of degree (like "incredibly") should come before the adverb of manner.

Correct sentence: She ran the marathon incredibly fast.

Additional Information

  • Types of Adverbs:
    • Adverbs of Manner: Describe how something happens (e.g., slowly, quickly).
    • Adverbs of Degree: Describe the intensity or degree of an action (e.g., very, incredibly).
  • Adverb Placement:
    • Example: She ran incredibly fast.
    • Rule: Place the adverb of degree before the adverb of manner for clarity and correctness.

questions.question: Direction: The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Select the segment that contains a grammatical error from the given options. I am going / to home / soon after the / programme gets over.
questions.questionHtml:
Direction: The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Select the segment that contains a grammatical error from the given options.

I am going / to home / soon after the / programme gets over.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'to home.'

Key Points

  • The error lies in Part (to home) of the sentence.
  • Going to is not a tense.
  • It is a special structure that we use to talk about the future.
  • "Home" is not a proper noun and it is an adverb of location.
  • "To" needs to be omitted.
  • ​Therefore, the use of 'to home' in the sentence should be replaced with 'home' to make it grammatically correct.
  • ​Correct sentence: I am going home soon after the programme gets over.

Additional Information  
 
 
 

  • We can use not … ever instead of never, but never is much more common.
    • Example: She has never been a friend of ours.

Hinglish   
 

  • त्रुटि वाक्य के Part (to home) में निहित है।
  • Going to, tense नहीं है।
  • यह एक विशेष संरचना है जिसका उपयोग हम भविष्य के बारे में बात करने के लिए करते हैं।
  • "Home" एक proper noun नहीं है और यह adverb of location है।
  • "To" को छोड़ना होगा।
  • इसलिए, वाक्य के 'to home' का उपयोग 'home' के साथ प्रतिस्थापित किया जाना चाहिए, इसे व्याकरणिक रूप से सही बनाने के लिए।

questions.question: From the given options, identify the segment in the sentence which contains the grammatical error. If the report did not have the information needed, it could not be used by them.
questions.questionHtml:
From the given options, identify the segment in the sentence which contains the grammatical error.

If the report did not have the information needed, it could not be used by them.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is If the​​.

Key Points​​

  • A conjunction is a word which is used to connect clauses or sentences or to coordinate words in the same clause.
  • We use 'Since' as a subordinating conjunction to introduce a subordinate clause.
  • We use it to give a reason for something.
  • Example:
    • Since her husband hated holidays so much, she decided to go on her own.
  • As per the possible context of the sentence, the report couldn't be used as it didn't have the required information.
  • In the given scenario, the conjunction 'Since' would serve the intended meaning better than the conjunction 'If'.
    ​

​Thus the correct sentence is: Since the report did not have the information needed, it could not be used by them.

 ​​​​Additional Information  ​

  • ​​The conjunction 'so...that' can be used instead of 'too...to' as given below:
    • She is too clumsy to handle glassware carefully.
    • ​She is so clumsy that she can't handle glassware carefully.

​

  • एक conjunction एक शब्द है जिसका उपयोग खंड या वाक्यों को जोड़ने या एक ही खंड में शब्दों के समन्वय के लिए किया जाता है।
  • हम एक एक अधीनस्थ खंड शुरू करने के लिए अधीनस्थ संयोजन, conjunction 'Since' का उपयोग करते हैं ।
  • हम इसका उपयोग किसी चीज का कारण देने के लिए करते हैं।
  • वाक्य के संभावित संदर्भ के अनुसार, रिपोर्ट का उपयोग नहीं किया जा सकता क्योंकि इसमें आवश्यक जानकारी नहीं थी।
  • दिए गए परिदृश्य में, 'Since' conjunction 'if' से बेहतर अर्थ में काम करेगा।

Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.

I hope that we will arrive at the ideal trade-off soon.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is "No Error". 

Key Points

  • The sentence structure is correct, with a main clause ("I hope that") and a subordinate clause ("we will arrive at the ideal trade-off soon").
  • Verb tenses and prepositions are correctly used.
  • Noun phrase and adverb are correctly positioned and used in the sentence.

Therefore, the correct answer is "Option 3". 

Additional Information 

  • Let's look at each part of the sentence:
    • "I hope that" is grammatically sound. The verb "hope" is correctly complemented by the connector "that," which introduces a subordinate clause expressing the content of the hope.
    • "we will arrive at" does not contain any grammatical mistakes. The future tense "will arrive" is appropriate because the speaker is expressing a hope about a future event. The preposition "at" is correctly used as well, since "arrive at" is a standard phrase meaning to reach a decision or an agreement.
    • "the ideal trade-off soon" is also grammatically correct. The noun phrase "the ideal trade-off" is a suitable object for the clause, indicated by the definite article "the," the adjective "ideal," and the compound noun "trade-off." The adverb "soon" correctly modifies the verb phrase "will arrive at," indicating when the speaker hopes the action will take place.

If a sentence is free from error, select 'No Error'. These ﬁve sisters (1)/ care for one another (2)/ like mothers. (3)/ No Error (4)/
questions.questionHtml:
In the following question, some part of the sentence may have errors. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. If a sentence is free from error, select 'No Error'. 

These ﬁve sisters (1)/ care for one another (2)/ like mothers. (3)/ No Error (4)/
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: No error.

Key Points

  • 'Each other' and 'one another' are reciprocal pronouns.
  • Reciprocal Pronouns are used to point out mutual relationship.
  • Each other: Each other is used when two persons are involved.
    • For example: Arnab and Raj are talking to each other.
  • One another: One another is used when more than two people are involved.
    • For example: The ten people were fighting amongst one another.
  • ​In this context, 'five sisters' are there. Hence, 'one another' are the correct pronouns used here.
  • The rest of the sentence is also grammatically correct.

Therefore, the correct answer is: No error.

questions.question: Identify the segment in the sentence, which contains the grammatical error. To be interested in the changing seasons is a happy state of mind than to be hopelessly in love with spring.
questions.questionHtml:
Identify the segment in the sentence, which contains the grammatical error.

To be interested in the changing seasons is a happy state of mind than to be hopelessly in love with spring.

options.text: than to be ho pelessly in love with spring
options.html: than to be hopelessly in love with spring

options.text: is a happy state of mind
options.html: is a happy state of mind

questions.solution:
The correct answer is "is a happy state of mind."
 
Key Points
  • The sentence contains a comparison indicating that one state of mind is better or more pleasant than the other.
  • Comparisons generally require the use of comparative adjectives.
  • The word "happy" should be in its comparative form "happier" to properly complete the comparison.
  • The phrase should read "is a happier state of mind" to indicate the comparative nature.
Therefore, the correct answer is: "Option 2".
 
Correct Sentence: To be interested in the changing seasons is a happier state of mind than to be hopelessly in love with spring.
 
Additional Information
  • than to be hopelessly in love with spring: This segment correctly contrasts two states of mind and properly uses "than" for comparison purposes.
  • To be interested: This part of the sentence correctly introduces one of the states being compared.
  • in the changing seasons: This segment properly completes the idea of one of the states of mind being discussed and is grammatically correct within the sentence.

questions.question: Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’. He always stood up for the rights of the oppressed.
questions.questionHtml:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’.

He always stood up for the rights of the oppressed.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 'No error'

Key Points

  • According to grammar, the sentence is grammatically correct.
  • The subject of the sentence is 'He' and the main verb of the sentence is 'stood up' also, 'for' is a preposition and 'the rights' is a prepositional object 'of' is a preposition 'the oppressed' is a prepositional object.
  • 'oppressed' is an adjective. Whenever an adjective written with a definite article it acts as a plural noun. So the meaning of 'the oppressed' here is 'the people who are distressed or anxious'

So the correct answer is- He always stood up for the rights of the oppressed.

questions.question: The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ in your answer. The river appears to have / got its name / from the town nearby.
questions.questionHtml:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ in your answer.

The river appears to have / got its name / from the town nearby.
questions.solution:
The correct No error.

Key Points

  • The use of the verb 'appears', meaning seem; give the impression of being, in the first part of the given sentence is grammatically correct as it follows a singular noun 'river'.
  • The use of the preposition 'to' in this context is also correct.
  • The use of the verb 'got' (past form of 'get') is also correct as the sentence indicates a past event, the time when the river got its name.
  • The use of the preposition 'from' in third part of the given sentence is also correct as it is indicating the point in space at which a journey, motion, or action starts, as in this case, the place where from the river got its name.
  • Therefore the given sentence is grammatically and contextually correct and free from any error.
  • Hence the correct answer is option 3.

Important Points

  • The perfect infinitive has the following structure: (to) have + past participle.
  • Examples are: to have missed, to have written, to have worked, to have left etc.
  • Perfect infinitives can have the same kind of meaning as perfect or past tenses.
    • I am glad to have found a new job. (= I am glad that I have found a new job.)

Confusion Points 

  • The past participle of the irregular verb “get” can be either “gotten” or “got,” depending on whether you're using UK or US English.

Therefore, the correct answer is "No error".

questions.solution:

Key Points

  • "Compromise" does not require "with" when it refers to negatively affecting or weakening something.

Therefore, the correct answer is: They compromise our health because they contain harmful preservatives.
